definition: To place two things side by side, especially so that their differences stand out.
example: The museum juxtaposed ancient clay bowls with modern ceramics to show how little the basic shapes had changed.
nuance: Compare can happen only in the mind; juxtapose means physically or textually setting things next to each other so the comparison shows.
prompt: A photographer is arranging her prints on a long gallery wall before an exhibit opens.
options: She decided to juxtapose a crowded city street with an empty desert road.
She wanted to juxtapose her largest print so it would fill the whole wall.
To juxtapose the two portraits, she hung them at opposite ends of the building.
Before the opening, she will juxtapose each print by signing the lower corner.
reasons: Hanging the two scenes next to each other makes the contrast between them sharp.
Enlarging one image involves no second item set beside it.
Moving the pictures far apart is the reverse of placing them side by side.
Adding a signature is not arranging one thing next to another.

practice.prompt: A novelist is planning the first chapter of a book about two very different families.
options: She tried to juxtapose her weak opening paragraph by deleting it entirely.
The chapter is meant to juxtapose that the quiet neighbor is secretly wealthy.
She plans to juxtapose the timeline so that every event happens in strict order.
She will juxtapose a lavish birthday feast with a family next door sharing cold soup.
reasons: Cutting a passage removes it; nothing ends up placed beside anything.
The verb needs two things to set together; it cannot announce a hidden fact.
Putting events in sequence is ordering them, not setting two elements in contrast.
Setting the scenes back to back makes the gap between plenty and want hard to miss.
